title: Divided Federal Reserve Holds Rates Steady as Three Officials Push for a Hike
summary: The US Federal Reserve kept its benchmark rate at 3.50%-3.75% in a 9-3 vote at Chair Kevin Warsh's second meeting, with three regional presidents dissenting in favour of an immediate rate increase as inflation stays elevated.
description: The Federal Reserve left its benchmark interest rate unchanged at a target range of 3.50% to 3.75% following its late-July meeting, the fifth consecutive hold, but the decision exposed a widening split on the policy committee. The vote was 9-3, with regional presidents Beth Hammack of Cleveland, Neel Kashkari of Minneapolis and Lorie Logan of Dallas dissenting because they wanted to raise rates now, arguing that inflation has stayed above the central bank's 2% target for years. It was the second meeting chaired by Kevin Warsh, who has described inflation as a policy choice and has favoured giving markets fewer explicit signals about the Fed's next move; the accompanying statement was again unusually brief. The committee said economic activity is expanding at a solid pace despite uncertainty tied to the Middle East conflict, while noting that inflation remains elevated. Stocks fell after the decision and Warsh's press conference, with the Dow dropping more than 800 points. The next policy meeting is scheduled for mid-September, following the Jackson Hole symposium in August.
image_alt: US Federal Reserve building representing the interest rate decision (illustrative)
key_points: The Fed held its benchmark rate at 3.50%-3.75% in a 9-3 vote.
Three regional presidents dissented, preferring an immediate rate hike.
It was Chair Kevin Warsh's second meeting, again featuring a short statement.
Stocks fell after the decision, with the Dow down more than 800 points.
why_it_matters: The Fed's rate stance drives borrowing costs on mortgages, credit cards and business loans, and the unusual level of dissent signals that another hike remains a live possibility later in 2026.

title: Big Tech Earnings Split Wall Street as Amazon Surges and Apple Slides
summary: Investors sorted the megacap technology names into winners and losers after results, sending Amazon sharply higher and Apple lower, as the market rewarded companies seen as best placed to profit from artificial intelligence.
description: A packed week of Big Tech results left Wall Street sharply divided, with investors rewarding the companies they view as clearer winners from the artificial intelligence boom and punishing those whose spending or strategy raised doubts. Amazon shares jumped in the wake of its report, helped by strength in its cloud-computing division, while Apple fell even after beating expectations, as some investors questioned its slower, more measured approach to AI. The divergence followed similar splits earlier in the week, when Microsoft rallied strongly and Meta Platforms slid on concerns about its AI plans and heavy capital spending. Analysts said the reaction underscored how selective the market has become: earnings beats alone are no longer enough, and guidance on AI investment and returns is now the key swing factor. Even so, the broader results season has been strong, with second-quarter profit growth for the S&P 500 tracking above 20% year over year, according to analyst estimates. The moves added to a volatile stretch shaped by Federal Reserve policy and geopolitical tensions.
image_alt: Stock market screen representing technology company earnings (illustrative)
key_points: Amazon shares surged after results while Apple fell despite beating expectations.
Microsoft rallied and Meta slid earlier in the week on differing AI views.
Investors increasingly reward companies seen as clear AI winners.
S&P 500 second-quarter earnings growth is tracking above 20% year over year.
why_it_matters: Megacap technology stocks carry heavy weight in major indexes and retirement portfolios, so how investors judge their AI strategies shapes returns for millions of savers.

title: US 30-Year Mortgage Rate Climbs to a One-Year High of 6.66%
summary: The average 30-year fixed US mortgage rate rose for a fourth straight week to 6.66%, its highest level in about a year, adding to affordability pressures for homebuyers as the Federal Reserve signals higher-for-longer policy.
description: The average rate on a 30-year fixed US mortgage climbed to 6.66% in the week ending July 30, according to Freddie Mac's weekly survey, up from 6.58% the previous week and its highest level in roughly a year. The 15-year fixed rate also rose, to 6.04%. It was the fourth consecutive weekly increase, and the move followed the Federal Reserve's decision to hold rates steady while signalling it may keep policy restrictive for longer. Analysts linked the rise to higher Treasury yields and stubborn inflation, with elevated energy prices tied to the Middle East conflict keeping the broader price picture unsettled; the 10-year Treasury yield, which mortgage rates tend to track, edged up after the Fed meeting. Higher borrowing costs add hundreds of dollars to monthly payments and erode purchasing power, and mortgage applications fell in the latest week as some buyers stepped back. Freddie Mac's chief economist noted that rising housing inventory is giving buyers more options and helping support activity even as rates fluctuate, but affordability remains strained heading into late summer.
image_alt: House keys and a model home representing mortgage borrowing costs (illustrative)
key_points: The 30-year fixed mortgage rate rose to 6.66%, a one-year high.
It was the fourth consecutive weekly increase; the 15-year rate reached 6.04%.
Higher Treasury yields and sticky inflation are pushing rates up.
Mortgage applications fell as elevated borrowing costs deter some buyers.
why_it_matters: Mortgage rates directly determine monthly payments and homebuying power, so a fresh one-year high tightens affordability for prospective buyers and dampens housing activity.

title: More US Health Insurers Retreat From ACA Marketplaces for 2027 as Premiums Rise
summary: Several insurers plan to exit Affordable Care Act marketplaces for 2027 and early rate filings point to steep premium increases, following the expiration of enhanced subsidies that had made coverage cheaper and driven record enrollment.
description: The outlook for the US individual health insurance market is tightening for 2027, according to tracking by health policy researchers. A number of carriers have announced plans to leave Affordable Care Act marketplaces in some or all of the states where they currently operate, while a smaller group intends to enter new states, and at least one large insurer has decided to exit the individual market entirely. At the same time, early rate filings from insurers point to sizeable premium increases for 2027, in many cases in the double digits. The pressure stems largely from the expiration at the end of 2025 of enhanced premium tax credits, which had lowered out-of-pocket costs and helped push enrollment to record highs; their lapse has raised what consumers pay and contributed to falling sign-ups. As membership shrinks, insurers are reassessing the profitability of marketplace participation, and in some regions fewer competing carriers will mean less choice for shoppers. Analysts warn that a smaller, potentially sicker risk pool could push premiums higher still, reinforcing a cycle of rising costs and declining coverage.
image_alt: Medical files and insurance paperwork representing health coverage changes (illustrative)
key_points: Several insurers plan to exit ACA marketplaces for 2027, reducing choice in some states.
Early 2027 rate filings point to double-digit premium increases.
The expiration of enhanced premium tax credits has raised consumer costs.
A smaller, sicker risk pool could push premiums higher still.
why_it_matters: Insurer exits and rising premiums leave many Americans who buy their own coverage with fewer options and higher costs, affecting the self-employed, small business owners and lower-income households most.

title: Bank of Japan Holds Rates at 1% but Warns Inflation Could Top 2% as Yen Sits Near 40-Year Low
summary: The Bank of Japan kept its policy rate at 1% and cautioned that core inflation could rise clearly above 2% later this fiscal year, as a yen hovering near a four-decade low fuelled speculation of government currency intervention.
description: The Bank of Japan left its benchmark policy rate unchanged at 1% at the conclusion of its two-day meeting, a widely expected decision that followed June's increase to the highest level since 1995. The vote was 8-1, with hawkish board member Hajime Takata dissenting in favour of raising the rate to 1.25% to guard against upside inflation risks. In its quarterly outlook, the central bank warned that core inflation was likely to accelerate to a level clearly above its 2% target in the second half of the fiscal year, citing wage increases feeding into prices, higher crude oil costs and a weaker yen, even though core inflation stood at 1.6% in July. The decision came amid intense focus on the currency, with the yen trading near a 40-year low against the dollar before spiking sharply, a move markets attributed to suspected intervention by Japanese authorities. Economists now debate whether the next rate increase arrives in October or December. Governor Kazuo Ueda's guidance at his press conference was closely parsed for clues on the pace of further tightening.
image_alt: Japanese yen banknotes representing central bank policy (illustrative)
key_points: The Bank of Japan held its policy rate at 1% in an 8-1 vote.
One board member dissented, seeking a hike to 1.25%.
The BOJ warned core inflation could rise clearly above 2% later this fiscal year.
The yen traded near a 40-year low, spurring talk of currency intervention.
why_it_matters: Japan's cautious tightening and a historically weak yen influence global bond markets, the cost of yen-funded investments and import prices for Japanese households.

title: UK's Big Banks Report Higher Half-Year Profits and Extend Buybacks
summary: Britain's largest lenders posted stronger first-half profits and continued returning cash to shareholders, buoyed by higher-for-longer interest rates, though some flagged the risk of rising bad loans linked to the conflict in the Middle East.
description: The UK's biggest banks delivered a run of stronger first-half results, helped by a higher-for-longer interest rate environment that has supported the margins they earn on lending. Lloyds Banking Group reported statutory pre-tax profit of about 4.3 billion pounds, up from 3.5 billion pounds a year earlier, with a banking net interest margin of 3.19% and progress on a multi-billion-pound share buyback. Rivals also updated the market during the reporting season, with Barclays and NatWest among those expected to show higher profits, and several lenders extending capital returns to shareholders through buybacks and dividends. Analysts noted that expectations for interest rates have swung sharply, with earlier hopes of cuts giving way to the prospect of increases after the inflation scare triggered by the US-Iran conflict, a shift that has helped bank revenues even as it squeezes borrowers. Still, some executives and analysts cautioned that the same economic backdrop, including higher energy costs and cost-of-living pressure, could push up impairment charges for bad loans in the quarters ahead, tempering the otherwise upbeat tone.
image_alt: Bank building facade representing UK lenders' earnings (illustrative)
key_points: Lloyds reported first-half statutory pre-tax profit of about 4.3 billion pounds, up from 3.5 billion.
Higher-for-longer interest rates supported bank lending margins.
Lenders extended share buybacks and dividends to return capital.
Some flagged the risk of rising bad loans tied to the Middle East conflict.
why_it_matters: Bank profitability affects savers, borrowers and shareholders alike, and lenders' warnings about loan quality offer an early read on how households and businesses are coping with higher costs.

title: Australian Inflation Eases in the Second Quarter, Easing Pressure on the RBA
summary: Australia's consumer inflation slowed by more than expected in the second quarter, with the closely watched core measure also moderating, offering the Reserve Bank of Australia some relief ahead of its August policy meeting.
description: Australia's inflation cooled by slightly more than forecast in the second quarter, giving the Reserve Bank of Australia room to stay patient before its next policy decision. Data from the Australian Bureau of Statistics showed annual headline inflation easing to about 3.9% from 4.1% in the previous quarter, while the trimmed mean, the central bank's preferred gauge of underlying price pressure, slowed to 3.6% year on year, below expectations. On a monthly basis, June inflation dropped to a four-month low of 3.8%, driven by softer goods prices as transport costs rose only marginally on falling fuel prices; housing and services inflation, however, remained firm. RBA Assistant Governor Sarah Hunter described the quarterly reading as a touch softer than expected, noting that underlying pressures from housing and services are proving persistent and that the labour market remains tight. The central bank's cash rate stands at 4.35%, with the next decision due in mid-August. Economists at major banks expect the RBA to keep rates on hold, with the softer data reducing the case for any near-term increase.
image_alt: City skyline representing Australia's economy and inflation data (illustrative)
key_points: Annual headline inflation eased to about 3.9% in the second quarter.
The trimmed mean core measure slowed to 3.6% year on year, below expectations.
June monthly inflation fell to a four-month low of 3.8%.
The RBA cash rate is 4.35%, with the next decision due in mid-August.
why_it_matters: Cooler inflation shapes whether the Reserve Bank raises, holds or eventually cuts rates, directly affecting mortgage costs and household budgets across Australia.

title: Singapore's MAS and Banks Form Taskforce to Counter AI-Driven Cyber Threats
summary: The Monetary Authority of Singapore and the Association of Banks in Singapore have set up a taskforce to strengthen the financial sector's cyber and technology resilience against threats amplified by advances in artificial intelligence.
description: The Monetary Authority of Singapore, together with the Association of Banks in Singapore, has established a taskforce to bolster the financial sector's resilience against cyber and technology threats that are being intensified by rapid advances in artificial intelligence. The move, highlighted around the release of the central bank's annual report, reflects mounting concern that increasingly capable AI models can be used to craft more sophisticated fraud, phishing and cyberattacks, while also raising the operational stakes of outages at banks, insurers and their technology providers. The taskforce is intended to coordinate the industry's response, share threat intelligence and develop practical measures to help institutions detect, prevent and recover from AI-enabled attacks. It builds on Singapore's broader agenda of promoting responsible AI adoption in finance alongside stronger cyber and operational-resilience standards, and complements recent cross-border cooperation, including an arrangement with Thailand's central bank to run joint cybersecurity exercises. For a global financial hub that has made digital innovation central to its strategy, the initiative underscores that safeguarding trust and system stability is viewed as a prerequisite for wider technology adoption rather than an afterthought.
image_alt: Cybersecurity systems representing defence against AI-driven threats (illustrative)
key_points: MAS and the Association of Banks in Singapore created a cyber-resilience taskforce.
It targets threats amplified by advances in artificial intelligence.
The group will coordinate response, share intelligence and set practical measures.
It follows recent cross-border cyber cooperation, including with Thailand's central bank.
why_it_matters: As banking and insurance move online, AI-enabled fraud and cyberattacks pose growing risks to customers and system stability, making stronger defences central to protecting people's money.

title: UAE Insurance Sector Premiums Jump 15.5% to Dh75.2 Billion
summary: Gross written premiums in the UAE's insurance sector rose 15.5% to about Dh75.2 billion, with total assets climbing to Dh166.7 billion, as the industry rode strong momentum in the country's non-oil economy.
description: The UAE's insurance sector extended a strong growth run, with gross written premiums rising 15.5% to about Dh75.2 billion and total assets climbing to roughly Dh166.7 billion, according to figures highlighted by the Central Bank of the UAE. The expansion reflects broader momentum in the country's non-oil economy, where financial and insurance services have been among the fastest-growing activities alongside manufacturing and construction. The central bank, which supervises insurers after the former Insurance Authority was merged into it, has been strengthening oversight and consumer protection across the sector as it grows. Rising premiums point to increased take-up of cover across life, health, motor and property lines, supported by population growth, economic diversification and greater awareness of insurance among residents and businesses. The performance comes as the wider UAE economy is projected to keep expanding at a solid pace, underpinned by government support measures and buoyant capital markets. Sustained double-digit premium growth positions the industry as an increasingly important part of the financial system, though regulators continue to emphasise solvency, fair treatment of policyholders and prudent underwriting as the market scales.
image_alt: Insurance documents representing the UAE insurance sector (illustrative)
key_points: UAE insurance gross written premiums rose 15.5% to about Dh75.2 billion.
Total sector assets climbed to roughly Dh166.7 billion.
Growth was supported by strong momentum in the non-oil economy.
The central bank continues to strengthen oversight and consumer protection.
why_it_matters: A fast-growing insurance market gives UAE residents and businesses wider access to protection, while its expansion makes the sector a larger pillar of the country's financial system.

title: IRDAI Approves Sweeping Reforms to Modernise India's Insurance Sector
summary: India's insurance regulator has approved a package of reforms aimed at strengthening governance, enhancing policyholder protection and speeding up insurance penetration, supporting the rollout of the amended insurance-law framework.
description: The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India has approved a wide-ranging set of reforms designed to modernise the country's insurance industry, strengthen governance and improve protection for policyholders while accelerating insurance penetration. The measures are intended to support implementation of the amended insurance-law framework enacted under the government's Sabka Bima Sabki Raksha initiative, which overhauls decades-old legislation. The regulator has framed insurance as a vital part of the economy that provides financial security, mobilises long-term savings and contributes to growth, and the reform package is part of a broader push toward its stated goal of insurance for all by 2047. Alongside governance and policyholder-protection measures, the regulator has been pursuing complementary changes, including steps to widen ownership, streamline product approvals, formalise stakeholder consultation and guide insurers on the responsible adoption of artificial intelligence with safeguards for data protection. Taken together, the reforms are aimed at making the sector more competitive, transparent and accessible, particularly in underserved markets, though much will depend on how effectively insurers and intermediaries implement the new requirements in the months ahead.
image_alt: Insurance policy and documents representing regulatory reform in India (illustrative)
key_points: IRDAI approved a package of reforms to modernise the insurance sector.
The measures strengthen governance and enhance policyholder protection.
They support the amended insurance-law framework under Sabka Bima Sabki Raksha.
The reforms align with the goal of insurance for all by 2047.
why_it_matters: Stronger rules on governance and policyholder protection, combined with efforts to widen access, could improve trust and coverage in a market where insurance penetration remains low.

title: Canada Reports May GDP and First Look at a Rebounding Second Quarter
summary: Statistics Canada released May economic output along with an early estimate for June, offering the first read on whether the economy returned to growth in the second quarter after two consecutive quarterly contractions.
description: Statistics Canada released figures for real gross domestic product in May, together with a flash estimate for June, giving the first clear picture of how the economy fared in the second quarter. Early indications had pointed to a modest 0.1% rise in May output, a slowdown from a solid 0.5% advance in April, as the economy worked through the drag from trade tensions and elevated borrowing costs. The May and June readings are significant because they follow two consecutive quarterly declines in real GDP, including a mild contraction in the first quarter that surprised the Bank of Canada and many economists. The results will help determine whether growth resumed over the April-to-June period or whether the economy remained under strain. Canada's central bank has held its policy rate at 2.25% amid uncertainty tied to shifting global trade relationships, and policymakers are watching output, jobs and inflation closely as they weigh the path ahead. A return to growth would ease concerns about a deeper slowdown, while continued weakness could strengthen the case for more supportive policy in the months to come.
image_alt: Port and shipping containers representing Canada's economic output (illustrative)
key_points: Statistics Canada reported May GDP and an early estimate for June.
Preliminary signals pointed to a modest 0.1% rise in May output.
The data follow two consecutive quarterly declines in real GDP.
The Bank of Canada has held its policy rate at 2.25% amid trade uncertainty.
why_it_matters: Whether Canada's economy returned to growth shapes expectations for interest rates and jobs, affecting borrowing costs and financial decisions for households and businesses.

title: South Korea's Economy Beats Forecasts in Q2 on a Semiconductor Export Boom
summary: South Korea's GDP grew 0.6% in the second quarter, double some forecasts, as a surge in semiconductor exports offset weaker construction, putting annual growth near 3% and strengthening the case for further rate action.
description: South Korea's economy expanded faster than expected in the second quarter, according to advance estimates from the Bank of Korea, as a boom in semiconductor exports offset a decline in construction investment. Real GDP rose 0.6% from the previous quarter, beating a median forecast of around 0.4% and far exceeding the central bank's own earlier projection, though the pace slowed from the first quarter's strong 1.8% expansion. On a year-on-year basis, output grew 3.7%, also topping expectations. Growth was driven by a gain in exports led by semiconductors, machinery and equipment, while private consumption rose modestly. A striking feature was real gross domestic income, which reflects the nation's purchasing power and jumped 15.6% year on year, its sharpest increase in nearly four decades, as robust chip shipments outweighed higher energy costs. Record monthly exports, which topped 100 billion dollars for the first time in June, underscored the strength of the technology cycle. The central bank has signalled it will likely raise its full-year growth outlook, and the strong momentum has reinforced expectations of additional interest rate moves.
image_alt: Semiconductor chip representing South Korea's export-driven growth (illustrative)
key_points: Second-quarter GDP grew 0.6% quarter on quarter, beating forecasts.
Annual growth reached 3.7%, driven by semiconductor exports.
Real gross domestic income surged 15.6%, its sharpest rise in decades.
The central bank is expected to raise its full-year growth outlook.
why_it_matters: South Korea is a bellwether for global technology demand, so its chip-led rebound signals the strength of the AI-driven export cycle while highlighting reliance on a single sector.

title: France Returns to Growth in the Second Quarter With Inflation Among the Lowest in the Euro Area
summary: France's economy grew modestly in the second quarter, contributing to a stronger-than-expected euro area, while French inflation stayed among the lowest in the bloc even as price pressures picked up across parts of Europe.
description: France's economy returned to growth in the second quarter, expanding about 0.2% from the previous quarter and helping the wider euro area outperform expectations. Eurostat's preliminary estimate showed euro area GDP rising 0.4%, up from flat growth at the start of the year and ahead of forecasts, suggesting the bloc has proved more resilient than feared despite higher energy prices and geopolitical uncertainty. Within that picture, growth has been uneven: Ireland and Spain led among European economies, while France, Germany and Italy expanded at a more modest pace. On inflation, France stood out at the lower end of the spectrum, with an annual rate of about 2.4% in July, among the lowest in the euro area, even as overall bloc-wide inflation edged up to 2.9% on the back of a sharp rise in energy costs. The combination of steady, if unspectacular, growth and relatively contained inflation gives French policymakers and the European Central Bank some breathing room, though officials remain watchful of energy-driven price pressures and the risks posed by the conflict in the Middle East.
image_alt: Paris cityscape representing the French economy (illustrative)
key_points: France's economy grew about 0.2% in the second quarter.
Euro area GDP rose 0.4%, beating expectations.
French annual inflation was about 2.4% in July, among the euro area's lowest.
Bloc-wide inflation edged up to 2.9%, driven by higher energy costs.
why_it_matters: Growth and inflation trends in France and the euro area shape European Central Bank policy, which affects borrowing costs, savings and investment across the bloc.

title: German Economy Lags as Euro Area Grows and Inflation Picks Back Up
summary: Germany expanded only marginally in the second quarter even as the wider euro area beat expectations, while early data pointed to German inflation rebounding in July, complicating the outlook for Europe's largest economy.
description: Germany, the euro area's largest economy, managed only marginal growth of around 0.1% in the second quarter, lagging a bloc that surprised to the upside. Eurostat's preliminary estimate showed euro area GDP expanding 0.4% from the previous quarter, up from flat growth earlier in the year and ahead of forecasts, with the strongest performances coming from smaller economies while Germany, France and Italy trailed. The subdued German reading underscores the structural challenges facing its manufacturing-heavy economy, from weak external demand to competitive pressure in key export markets. Adding to the complexity, early inflation data suggested price pressures are re-emerging: economists estimated that German headline inflation rebounded to roughly 2.7% to 2.8% in July, up from June, after regional readings showed firmer price growth across several states. The pickup echoes a broader trend, with euro area inflation edging up to 2.9% on higher energy costs. For policymakers, the mix of tepid German growth and firmer inflation is awkward, limiting room for support even as the economy struggles to gain momentum, though officials expect fiscal stimulus to help later in the year.
image_alt: German cityscape representing Europe's largest economy (illustrative)
key_points: Germany grew only about 0.1% in the second quarter, lagging the euro area.
Euro area GDP rose 0.4%, beating expectations.
German inflation was estimated to rebound to around 2.7%-2.8% in July.
Firmer inflation limits room for policy support despite weak growth.
why_it_matters: As Europe's largest economy, Germany's weak growth and renewed inflation shape the region's outlook and the European Central Bank's policy, with knock-on effects for jobs and borrowing costs.

title: UAE Banking Sector Assets Climb 17.7% to AED 5.56 Trillion
summary: The UAE's banking sector recorded robust growth, with total assets rising 17.7% year on year to AED 5.56 trillion and lending up more than 20%, while banks maintained strong capital buffers, the central bank reported.
description: The UAE's banking sector posted robust growth, with total assets rising 17.7% year on year to about AED 5.56 trillion, according to the Central Bank of the UAE. The loan portfolio expanded by 20.3% over the same period, while deposits grew 17.4%, reflecting strong credit demand and healthy liquidity as the country's non-oil economy continued to expand. Banks maintained solid balance sheets, with the capital adequacy ratio at 16.8%, pointing to ample buffers to absorb potential shocks, alongside improved asset quality. The central bank kept its base rate at 3.65%, in line with US Federal Reserve policy, given the dirham's peg to the dollar, and market interest rates broadly tracked that benchmark. The banking sector's strength has been underpinned by momentum in financial services, construction and trade, as well as government support measures and an expanding network of trade agreements. Sustained double-digit growth in assets and lending highlights the sector's central role in financing the UAE's diversification drive, though regulators continue to emphasise prudent risk management, strong capital positions and sound governance as the system scales.
image_alt: Dubai skyline representing the UAE banking sector (illustrative)
key_points: UAE banking sector total assets rose 17.7% year on year to about AED 5.56 trillion.
The loan portfolio grew 20.3% and deposits rose 17.4%.
The capital adequacy ratio stood at 16.8%, indicating strong buffers.
The central bank kept its base rate at 3.65%, tracking US Fed policy.
why_it_matters: A fast-growing, well-capitalised banking sector supports lending to households and businesses and underpins the UAE's economic diversification, while strong buffers help protect the financial system.
